marble.name: Surface area using nets
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Represent right rectangular prisms, triangular prisms and pyramids with rectangular or triangular bases using nets made of rectangles and triangles; use the solid's dimensions to label every face on the net; find the surface area as the sum of the face areas, in square units; distinguish surface area (the area covering
marble.prompt: If you wants to wrap a shoebox 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm tall, could they sketch the box unfolded flat, work out the area of each rectangle and add them up to find how much paper is needed?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning about measurement in everyday life — telling time to the hour and half-hour, comparing lengths and weights of objects, understanding money, and using time words like yesterday and tomorrow.

misconceptions: 'Surface area is length times width times height.'
authoredAnswer: Open area 15+2×10+2×6=47 cm²; lid adds 15 for 62 cm² closed. Draws five/six correct faces with square units.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Uses a cubic-volume product for a covering task. Source basis: NCETM, KS3 6.2 Perimeter, area and volume, overview and representations. The child-voice wording is an authored diagnostic adaptation, not a study quotation.
wrongAnswers.fix: Label face areas on the net and sum them; contrast square covering with cubic packing.

before.name: Area of Triangles & Parallelograms
before.reason: Pyramid and triangular-prism nets contain triangular faces whose areas are needed; rectangle area comes with it

before.name: Volume of cuboids
before.reason: Knowing volume as cubes filling a solid helps learners distinguish it from surface area (square units covering the outside)

before.name: Nets of 3-D Shapes
before.reason: Surface area is found from a net, so learners must be able to draw and interpret nets of prisms and pyramids

after.name: Surface area and volume of solids
